```{python}
#| echo: false
import duckdb

con = duckdb.connect("../data/whoop.duckdb", read_only=True)
con.sql("set TimeZone = 'UTC'")

def one(sql):
    return con.sql(sql).fetchall()[0][0]

PRIMARY = "from fct_decision_points where is_in_primary_analysis"
n_people = one(f"select count(distinct participant_id) {PRIMARY}")
n_dp = one(f"select count(*) {PRIMARY}")
n_outcome = one(f"select count(*) {PRIMARY} and has_outcome")
n_sent = one(f"select count(*) {PRIMARY} and is_sent")
p_walk = one(f"select avg(coalesce(is_sent_walking, false)::int) {PRIMARY}")
p_sed = one(f"select avg(coalesce(is_sent_anti_sedentary, false)::int) {PRIMARY}")
n_travel = one("select count(*) from fct_decision_points where is_randomized and is_during_travel")
n_zero = one(f"select count(*) {PRIMARY} and steps_30m_after = 0")
miss_sent = one(f"select avg((not has_outcome)::int) {PRIMARY} and is_sent")
miss_not = one(f"select avg((not has_outcome)::int) {PRIMARY} and not is_sent")
```

## Result: `{python} r["decision"]`, under the pre-registered rule

A suggestion increased steps in the next 30 minutes by **`{python} est(prim)`**, about `{python} f"{prim['steps']:+.0f}"` steps on a `{python} f"{r['baseline_steps']:.0f}"`-step average, with no guardrail flags. The effect is real but fragile and short-lived: the confidence interval only just excludes zero, and the effect fades to nothing within about a month.
:::

## Results

The analysis below follows the plan further down this page exactly. The plan was committed first (e39c0a7) and the results second (b3e15ea); there are no deviations.

### The headline, and how confident to be

- **Primary:** `{python} est(prim)`, p = `{python} f"{prim['p']:.3f}"`. The published analysis of the same trial found +14% (p = .06), so the two agree closely.
- **Sensitivity:** treating missing step counts as zero gives `{python} est(zf)`, p = `{python} f"{zf['p']:.3f}"`. The same evidence lands on either side of p = .05 depending on how missing data is handled, so the effect should be read as modest and uncertain, not as proven.

### The effect fades

```{python}
#| echo: false
curve = r["by_day_curve"]
days = list(curve)
mid = [curve[d]["pct"] for d in days]
lo = [curve[d]["pct_lo"] for d in days]
hi = [curve[d]["pct_hi"] for d in days]
fig = go.Figure([
    go.Scatter(x=days + days[::-1], y=hi + lo[::-1], fill="toself", fillcolor="rgba(99,110,250,0.18)",
               line=dict(width=0), hoverinfo="skip", name="95% CI"),
    go.Scatter(x=days, y=mid, line=dict(width=3, color="#636EFA"), name="Estimated effect"),
])
fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dot")
fig.update_layout(title="Extra steps from a suggestion, by day of the study",
                  xaxis_title="Study day", yaxis_title="% change in 30-minute steps",
                  margin=dict(t=70), legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="top", y=-0.2, x=0))
fig.show(config={"displayModeBar": False})
```

On the first day a suggestion added `{python} est(d0)`. By day 20 it was `{python} est(d20)`, and by day 30 `{python} est(d30)`, no longer distinguishable from zero. The model assumes a straight-line decline, so the exact shape is an approximation; the decline itself is clear (`{python} f"{r['decay_slope']['pct']:+.1f}"`% per day, p = `{python} f"{r['decay_slope']['p']:.3f}"`) and matches the published finding that the effect started large and faded.

### What worked and what did not

```{python}
#| echo: false
rows = [("Primary: any suggestion", prim, 14.0), ("Missing = 0 steps", zf, None),
        ("Day 0 of the study", d0, None), ("Day 30 of the study", d30, None),
        ("Walking suggestions", walk, 24.0), ("Anti-sedentary suggestions", sed, None),
        ("At home or work", r["home_or_work"], None), ("Elsewhere", r["elsewhere"], None)]
labels = [n for n, _, _ in rows]
fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=[e["pct"] for _, e, _ in rows], y=labels, mode="markers", marker=dict(size=10, color="#636EFA"),
    error_x=dict(type="data", symmetric=False,
                 array=[e["pct_hi"] - e["pct"] for _, e, _ in rows],
                 arrayminus=[e["pct"] - e["pct_lo"] for _, e, _ in rows]),
    name="This analysis"))
pub = [(n, v) for n, _, v in rows if v is not None]
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[v for _, v in pub], y=[n for n, _ in pub], mode="markers",
                         marker=dict(symbol="diamond-open", size=13, color="#EF553B"),
                         name="Published (Klasnja et al., 2019)"))
fig.add_vline(x=0, line_dash="dot")
fig.update_layout(title="Effect on 30-minute steps, with 95% CIs", xaxis_title="% change",
                  yaxis=dict(autorange="reversed"), margin=dict(l=200, t=70),
                  legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="top", y=-0.2, x=0))
fig.show(config={"displayModeBar": False})
```

Walking suggestions worked (`{python} est(walk)`; published +24%). Anti-sedentary suggestions did not (`{python} est(sed)`). Location made no clear difference: both intervals cross zero.

### Guardrails

```{python}
#| echo: false
gw = g.loc[1:6]
fig = go.Figure([go.Scatter(x=gw.index, y=100 * gw[c], mode="lines+markers", name=n)
                 for c, n in [("bad", "Rated bad"), ("no_response", "No response"), ("snoozed", "Snoozed")]])
fig.update_layout(title="How participants responded to suggestions, by study week",
                  xaxis_title="Study week", yaxis_title="% of suggestions sent", yaxis_range=[0, 40],
                  margin=dict(t=70), legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="top", y=-0.2, x=0))
fig.show(config={"displayModeBar": False})
```

No guardrail was flagged. "Bad" ratings went from `{python} f"{100 * g.loc[1, 'bad']:.1f}"`% in week 1 to `{python} f"{100 * g.loc[6, 'bad']:.1f}"`% in week 6, "no response" from `{python} f"{100 * g.loc[1, 'no_response']:.1f}"`% to `{python} f"{100 * g.loc[6, 'no_response']:.1f}"`%, and snoozes never passed `{python} f"{100 * g['snoozed'].max():.1f}"`%.

The more useful finding is what the guardrails missed: ratings stayed flat while the effect itself disappeared. Participants stopped acting on suggestions without telling anyone they were tired of them.

### What this means for WHOOP

1. **Test proactive check-ins, and plan for the fade.** Measure the effect by week, not just overall; a check-in that works in week one may do nothing by week five.
2. **Make the ask specific.** Walking suggestions, which named an action, worked; generic "get up and move" prompts did not.
3. **Do not rely on ratings as the fatigue guardrail.** Track the behavioural effect itself over time, and in a member-level test also track opt-outs and churn, which this design could not compare.
4. **Size the test for a small effect.** If the WHOOP effect is in this range, the test needs many members; the [power analysis](memo.qmd) works out how many.

### Notes on implementation

- "Last full study week" in the guardrail rule was taken as **week 6**, because the trial ran six weeks; weeks 7 to 9 contain only `{python} f"{int(g.loc[7:, 'sent'].sum()):,}"` suggestions from a few late participants.
- Average steps are reported for decision points with no suggestion (`{python} f"{r['baseline_steps']:.0f}"`); the published 253 was an average over all decision points, so the step figures are close but not identical in definition.

# Analysis plan (written before the results)


## The decision this informs

WHOOP is adding proactive features such as Coach check-ins. The question for a product team is whether an unprompted nudge changes what members do soon after it arrives, and whether that is worth building and testing on WHOOP members. This readout cannot answer that for WHOOP directly. It uses a public trial to estimate whether nudges like this work at all, how large the effect is, and whether it fades, so that a WHOOP A/B test can be sized and designed well.

## The experiment

HeartSteps V1 was a six-week trial with sedentary adults. Five times a day, at moments when a participant was available (not driving, phone connected, not already exercising), the app randomly decided whether to send an activity suggestion. Each person was randomized hundreds of times, so every participant contributes to both arms. This design is called a micro-randomized trial.

- **Participants:** `{python} n_people` (the published analysis sample)
- **Randomized decision points:** `{python} f"{n_dp:,}"`, excluding `{python} f"{n_travel:,}"` during participants' travel, as in the published analysis
- **Suggestions sent:** `{python} f"{n_sent:,}"` (`{python} f"{100 * n_sent / n_dp:.1f}"`%; the design was 60%)

## Hypothesis

Sending an activity suggestion at an available decision point increases the number of steps taken in the next 30 minutes, compared with sending nothing.

## Primary metric

**Steps in the 30 minutes after the decision point**, from the wrist tracker, analyzed as log(steps + 0.5) because step counts are heavily skewed. Results are reported as a percentage change and as extra steps at the average.

## Analysis method

- **Model:** regression of the primary metric on the treatment indicator centred at its randomization probability (sent minus 0.6), controlling for log steps in the 30 minutes before. Because the randomization probability is constant, this is the weighted and centred least squares estimator built for micro-randomized trials, with all weights equal to 1.
- **Uncertainty:** standard errors clustered by participant, with a t distribution on `{python} n_people - 1` degrees of freedom, because there are only `{python} n_people` people and their decision points are not independent.
- **Missing outcome:** the primary analysis uses decision points with a recorded 30-minute step count (`{python} f"{n_outcome:,}"` of `{python} f"{n_dp:,}"`). The file already records `{python} f"{n_zero:,}"` windows as zero steps, so a missing value means no tracker data rather than no walking. Missing outcomes are balanced between arms in this sample (`{python} f"{100 * miss_not:.1f}"`% with no suggestion vs `{python} f"{100 * miss_sent:.1f}"`% with one), which is what makes a complete-case comparison fair. A missing "before" count is set to zero with an indicator added to the model.
- **Sensitivity analysis:** repeat the primary model treating every missing outcome as zero steps.

## Pre-specified secondary analyses

1. **Does the effect fade?** Add an interaction between treatment and study day.
2. **Does the type of suggestion matter?** Walking suggestions and anti-sedentary ("get up and move") suggestions, each compared with no suggestion. The public files do not document the per-type randomization probabilities, so they are estimated from the data (walking `{python} f"{100 * p_walk:.0f}"`%, anti-sedentary `{python} f"{100 * p_sed:.0f}"`% of decision points) and used for centring.
3. **Does location matter?** Home or work versus elsewhere.

Anything else looked at later is labelled exploratory. Secondary results are treated as hypotheses for WHOOP's own test, not as proven.

## Guardrails

A micro-randomized trial gives every participant both arms, so person-level guardrails such as dropout or uninstalling cannot be compared between arms here. A member-level A/B test at WHOOP could compare them, and should. What this trial can track is how participants rated the suggestions they received, week by week:

| Guardrail | Flag if |
|---|---|
| Share of sent suggestions rated "bad" | rises by more than 10 points from the first to the last full study week |
| Share of sent suggestions with no response | rises by more than 10 points from the first to the last full study week |
| Share of sent suggestions snoozed | above 5% in any week |

## Decision rule

| Result | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| Primary effect positive, 95% CI excludes zero, no guardrail flags | **Go:** build proactive check-ins and run a member-level A/B test |
| Primary CI includes zero, but a pre-specified secondary analysis shows a positive effect with a CI excluding zero (for example early weeks only, or walking suggestions only); or a positive primary effect with a guardrail flag | **Go with changes:** test only the version that worked, with a frequency cap |
| No pre-specified analysis shows a positive effect with a CI excluding zero | **No go:** do not build on this evidence |

## Benchmark

The published primary analysis (Klasnja et al., 2019) found that a suggestion increased 30-minute steps by 14% (p = .06), about 35 steps over a 253-step average, with an effect that started larger and faded over time. Walking suggestions increased steps by 24% (p = .02); anti-sedentary suggestions had no detectable effect. I expect to land near these numbers. The most likely source of any difference is missing data: the published analysis imputed missing step counts, while this one uses complete cases and reports zero-filling as a sensitivity check.

## What this cannot tell us

- **WHOOP members are not these participants.** These were sedentary adults in 2015 receiving walking prompts; WHOOP members are active and the behaviour that matters may be training, not walking.
- **Thirty minutes is not retention.** A short-term step bump does not show that nudges bring lapsed members back. The [power analysis](memo.qmd) sizes the WHOOP test that would answer that.
